page_summary:
The Crack in Space is the canonical works record for PKD's novel. It preserves a single archive manifestation and gives the work a stable bibliographic home. The preserved item here is The Crack in Space (Knopf Doubleday Edition) (1966).

Researchers can use this entry to trace publication context, later commentary, and relationships to other works.

structure.form: novel intercutting a political campaign plot with the discovery and contested exploitation of a parallel-world resettlement opportunity

characters.name: Jim Briskin
characters.note: The first Black candidate for the American presidency, campaigning partly on a promise to resettle the country's chronically unemployed, cryogenically suspended underclass to the newly discovered parallel Earth.

settings.name: Overcrowded near-future America
settings.note: Grappling with chronic unemployment and racial tension, with much of its underclass held in long-term cryogenic suspension for lack of jobs or housing.

settings.name: The parallel Earth beyond the crack
settings.note: Discovered via a malfunctioning instantaneous transit device, initially believed empty and available for human resettlement, but revealed to harbor its own indigenous hominid population.

motifs: Technological accident opening unexpected political and social opportunity, immediately contested by competing factions
Resettlement and colonization premised on an assumption of emptiness that turns out to be false, echoing real-world colonial displacement of indigenous populations
Racial politics and a historic first Black presidential candidacy intersecting directly with a science-fictional resource crisis
Cryogenic suspension as a literal, institutionalized holding pattern for economically surplus populations
reading.significance: The Crack in Space, expanded from Dick's 1964 novella Cantata 140, is notable for its direct engagement with contemporary American racial politics through Jim Briskin's historic candidacy, years before a Black presidential candidacy became a mainstream political possibility in reality. Its parallel-world resettlement plot, complicated by the discovery of an indigenous population the human characters had assumed did not exist, functions as a pointed science-fictional allegory for the colonial premise that supposedly empty land is available for the taking, undercutting the technological-solution optimism of its own premise with an ethical complication its characters did not anticipate.
reading.closing_note: The discovery of the parallel Earth's indigenous population leaves the resettlement plan's moral and political legitimacy as unresolved as the overcrowding crisis it was meant to solve.
